MARCUS: Okay, so — I want to ask you about the shop, the one on Blackstone. When did you actually open that?

FRANK: Which shop.

MARCUS: The one — Dad, the hardware store. Delgado's.

FRANK: Oh, that wasn't a shop, that was your grandfather's, I just worked there summers. You're thinking of the wrong — wait, no, actually you might be right, did I tell you about that?

MARCUS: No?

FRANK: Huh. Well anyway. Sixty-eight, I think, or somewhere in there, your grandfather — Pop — he leased the space from a Armenian fella, Zakarian, I want to say, and he — hold on, this is a good story actually — he almost didn't get the lease because the landlord thought Pop was too young to run a business, he was like twenty-six —

MARCUS: Twenty-six.

FRANK: Twenty-six, twenty-seven, somewhere there, and so Pop brings his own father — your great-grandfather, who you never met, Salvador — brings him to the meeting just to stand there and look serious. Didn't say a word. Just stood there. And that's what got him the lease, apparently. Presence. [laughs] Your great-grandfather had presence.

MARCUS: That's — okay, we're getting off track, I wanted to ask about —

FRANK: No, no, this is relevant, hold on —

MARCUS: [laughing] Dad —

FRANK: — because that's actually how I ended up working there, is the thing, because Pop believed in that, showing up, presence, and he made me and your uncle Ray come stand around the shop even when we were like eleven, twelve years old, just to — I don't know what he thought we were doing, learning by osmosis I guess —

MARCUS: Did you like it? The shop.

FRANK: The smell of it, yeah. Cut wood, and there was a — this is gonna sound strange — there was a specific kind of oil they used on the saw blades, I could probably still identify it blindfolded. Carol used to say I smelled like the shop even after I stopped working there, years after, she'd say "you still smell like Blackstone Avenue" —

[pause]

MARCUS: You okay?

FRANK: Yeah. Yeah, I'm — she used to say that. Anyway.

MARCUS: We don't have to —

FRANK: No, no, it's fine, I like — actually I like talking about her, people think you shouldn't bring it up but I'd rather you bring it up than not.

MARCUS: Okay. Good — I mean, not good, but. Good to know.

FRANK: [laughs] Good to know. Christ.

MARCUS: So — Blackstone. What happened to the shop eventually?

FRANK: Oh, it closed, this was — must've been eighty-one, eighty-two, Home Depot type places started coming in, the big — what were they called before Home Depot, there was a regional one —

MARCUS: I don't know, Dad.

FRANK: Builders Square, maybe? Something like that. Anyway they came in and Pop couldn't compete on the prices, and — you know what's funny, actually, is that Ray wanted to sue somebody over this, he had some idea that it was unfair competition, some legal — Ray always had these ideas, you remember Ray —

MARCUS: I met Uncle Ray twice.

FRANK: Right, right, he moved to Reno. Anyway nothing came of the lawsuit thing, obviously, but Pop was never really the same after the shop closed, he'd go down there — this is the sad part I guess — he'd go down there after it was already somebody else's business, a check-cashing place I think it became, and just stand outside it. Never went in. Just stood there a minute and then walked home.

MARCUS: Did he ever say why?

FRANK: Never asked him. [pause] Should've asked him, probably. That's — you know, that's actually a good — is that the kind of thing you're after? Because I got a million of these, I don't know if they're useful to you or if you wanted more like, the big events, the — what's the word — milestones.

MARCUS: No, this is exactly it, actually.

FRANK: Yeah? Okay, well — oh, you know what I never told you, this is a good one, about the day I met your mother, do you know this story —

MARCUS: I know the dance hall one.

FRANK: No, before the dance hall, there was a — okay so before I even talked to her, I saw her at, this'll sound made up, I saw her at a laundromat, and I did not talk to her, I was too nervous, and I went home and told my mother, your grandmother, that I'd met the woman I was gonna marry, and I hadn't even said one word to her —

MARCUS: [laughing] Wait, that's not the story you usually tell.

FRANK: Well I'm telling you the real one now! The dance hall thing came after, that's just where I actually introduced myself, but the laundromat's where I saw her first, and I never told anybody that part because it sounds — I don't know, it sounds like I'm making it up, but I swear to god —

MARCUS: I believe you.

FRANK: — I went home and I told my mother, I said "Ma, I found her," and she said "found who," and I said "the one I'm gonna marry," and she laughed at me, she thought it was — you know, seventeen-year-old nonsense. And I was right though. Eventually. Took me about four months to actually talk to her.

MARCUS: Four months of what, following her around laundromats?

FRANK: [laughs] No — no, I found out she went to the dances at the Rainbow Ballroom, so I started going, and it took me that long to get the nerve up. Your mother, when I finally did talk to her, she said she'd clocked me weeks before and was wondering when I'd get around to it.

MARCUS: Of course she was.

FRANK: Of course she was, yeah. She was never gonna make the first move, that wasn't her nature, but she was not gonna wait forever either, she told me later she'd given me like one more week before she was gonna find somebody else to dance with.

MARCUS: That's — I've never heard the laundromat part, that's a good one.

FRANK: Yeah, well. Some of these I just never — you don't think to tell them, you know? It's not like it comes up. Nobody asks "hey Dad, did you ever stalk Mom at a laundromat," that's not a normal question somebody asks.

MARCUS: [laughing] I mean, I'm asking it now.

FRANK: Well now you know. Write that one down.
